questions.q: Why does a new engineering standard announced via a Slack message and a linked document often fail to actually change behavior?
options: Documents are always factually incorrect when they describe new standards
Slack messages are technically incapable of containing useful information

Reading a document and changing a habit are different things, and nothing about a one-time announcement closes that gap -- people default back to old habits under time pressure unless something in the workflow enforces the change
Teams never read documents that are shared with them
questions.explain: An announcement alone doesn't make the new standard the easier path in someone's actual daily workflow -- without reinforcement, people quietly revert to existing habits.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend tooling-enforced standards (CI checks, linters) over standards that depend on a human reviewer remembering to check?
options: There is no real difference in consistency between the two approaches

Tooling-enforced standards get followed consistently because they don't depend on anyone remembering anything, while human-enforced standards are followed inconsistently since reviewers are busy, tired, or new
Tooling-enforced standards are always technically impossible to implement
Human reviewers always catch every violation of a standard without exception
questions.explain: A CI check that blocks a pull request doesn't depend on anyone's memory or attention in the moment -- it closes the gap that human vigilance alone leaves open.

questions.q: Why does a standard delivered as a finished document from the senior engineer, with no team input, tend to be followed resentfully or not at all?
options: Standards delivered by senior engineers are always technically wrong
A standard the team was never consulted about and merely tolerates has less real ownership than one the team helped shape, even if the content is identical
Teams always actively sabotage any standard regardless of how it's introduced
There is no real difference in how a standard is received based on how it was introduced
questions.explain: Bringing the PROBLEM to the team first and letting them help shape the standard produces real ownership; handing down a finished rule produces mere tolerance, even for an identically good standard.

questions.q: What is the difference between a 'hard requirement' and a 'strong default,' as the lesson defines them?
options: Hard requirements are only used for documentation standards, never for anything else
A hard requirement and a strong default are identical concepts with different names
A strong default is always more strictly enforced than a hard requirement

A hard requirement is enforced with no exceptions because the cost of letting it slide is high; a strong default is usually followed but allows a conscious, explained exception when a specific situation warrants one
questions.explain: The distinction is about how much room for judgment the standard allows -- universal, high-cost-if-skipped rules should be hard requirements; usually-right but not universal rules work better as strong defaults.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn that applying a rigid, zero-exception standard to EVERY possible case tends to backfire?
options: Rigid standards have no real effect on team behavior either way
Someone eventually hits a real case the rule wasn't designed for, which tends to produce workarounds and quiet non-compliance rather than genuine adherence
Rigid standards always produce perfect compliance with no downsides
This only applies to standards that are tooling-enforced, never human-enforced ones
questions.explain: A rule with zero room for judgment eventually meets a legitimate edge case it wasn't designed to handle -- at that point, people route around it instead of following it, which undermines the standard more than a reasonable exception would have.
